title: CLO Master Express Lesson 28 | How to Creatively Display Your Virtual Garments
description: Learn how to fold, arrange, and hang your virtual garments in CLO to upgrade your display style!!
transcript:
Hello everyone, I’m Samantha. Long time no see. Tonight, I will bring you a live demonstration of garment presentation techniques. Here, I will teach you how to do hanging garments, folded garments, and styling.

First, let’s talk about hanging garments—how to hang clothes on a hanger.

First, we import the finished upper garment.

Next, we need to adjust the garment’s particle distance to 10 and increase thickness collision to 2. This is to allow a faster simulation, making it easier to hang the clothes on the hanger.

Now, we simulate using the adjusted parameters.

Then, we import the hanger. The system provides various types of hangers, and you can choose according to your needs.

Here, we can move the garment onto the hanger using our positioning tool.

After adjusting the position, we can start the simulation.

While simulating on the hanger, we can select our garment.

During simulation, sometimes the garment may penetrate the hanger.

In this case, simply use the move tool to gently drag the fabric of the garment back outside the hanger to prevent penetration.

We can also slightly adjust the hanging position of the garment, for example, pulling the shoulder area a little to reposition it.

This completes the hanging of the upper garment, and next, we improve its quality.

Next, let’s talk about how to create the effect of pants clipped onto a hanger.

First, import a finished pair of jeans.

Similarly, adjust the particle distance and collision thickness. Since we will fix the waistband to the clip with pins later, we only need to adjust the main body parameters of the pants.

Set particle distance to 10 and collision thickness to 2.

After adjustment, simulate using these parameters, then delete the avatar.

Use the 3D garment folding tool to lay out the pants flat.

First, rotate along the X-axis to quickly place the pants centered on the floor.

Then set the folding physical properties, which will make the pants very soft and convenient for laying flat on the ground.

After simulation, the pants will quickly lay flat on the ground.

Simulate again so the waistband is also laid flat.

Next, adjust the waistband’s flat effect so the front and back waist overlap.

After finishing, remember to turn off the folding physical properties. This allows the correct physical properties of the jeans to apply to the pants.

Next, import the hanger with clips.

Select the pants’ panels and adjust their position to align with the clips on the hanger.

You can adjust the pants’ position from the front view to approximate the effect of hanging on the clip.

Zoom in on the clip area and fine-tune the pants’ position.

Since we clip the waistband first, push the waistband inward to leave more space, and also position the front waist properly.

Check from front and back views for any penetration issues and verify the overall position.

If everything is fine, next, use pins to fix the pants onto the clips.

First, add pins in the 3D window to help locate pin positions in the 2D window.

Because the waistband is curved, use the lasso pin tool to select the pinning area.

Here, since the waistband includes a label and three layers (outer, inner, and pants), we need to pin all three layers to fix them securely.

Next, pin the other clip on the hanger the same way—draw the open position in the 3D window, then find and pin the corresponding panels in the 2D window.

Now both sides’ pins are added.

Also add pins on the side seams and above the waistband to help pull the pants’ sides straight later.

After pinning, simulate.

You will notice the clip area moving a lot. Since we increased the avatar surface distance (avatar collision offset), we need to adjust it.

Multiply the offset by 3 and set it to 0, creating more space in the clip area for fabric simulation.

Now, the fabric does not move excessively.

If there is penetration, adjust accordingly. Because pins make it easier to move fabric, extra care is needed when dragging during simulation.

For fabric penetration that cannot be dragged out, use the “reverse activation” or “avatar toggle” method: deactivate the avatar temporarily, simulate again, then reactivate. This solves penetration issues.

You can adjust pin positions during simulation to allow more space for the front waist.

If there is penetration near the label or pin area bulging, remove the pins there and simulate again to fix it.

If penetration persists, try removing some pins on the front or back waist, as they may be causing fabric to stretch out.

When dragging pins, you can hide them to avoid accidentally moving them.

After adjusting pins, show them again and check for penetration.

If none, proceed to the next step.

Next, adjust the side seam pins of the pants to straighten the sides.

Adjust the other side the same way: first adjust the front view for realistic placement, then check front/back position in the 2D window.

Start simulation and adjust pin positions.

The pants will be stretched flat, making the hanging effect on the clips look cleaner.

Next, add a pin in the front center to slightly scrunch the fabric since the front center may hang down too much.

After adjusting the waist position, add pins to the front waist panels, moving them into the clips in the 3D window.

In the 2D window, adjust the pin range accordingly.

Add the same pins on the other side.

Adjust pin positions and simulate.

Note: pins should not pass through the clips too quickly, as this causes fabric-avatar conflicts.

Adjust positions to be in front of the clips without penetration.

Deactivate the hanger’s avatar temporarily, then activate simulation with the pins inside the clips.

Fine-tune pin vertical positions, avoiding pressing too far back to prevent avatar clipping issues.

Adjust pins on the other side similarly.

Check front view for symmetry in height.

Adjust if asymmetrical.

Reactivate avatar and simulate.

During simulation, you can further adjust pin positions to improve clip appearance and prevent excessive sagging.

After adjustments, remove the pins on the waistband side seams and front center to allow natural simulation.

Check for penetration issues and adjust by dragging fabric out.

If large penetrations are hard to drag, hide the avatar and check pins for blocking fabric movement.

Adjust pins and try detaching fabric.

If still unresolved, use reverse activation of the avatar again.

After final simulation, penetration problems should be resolved.

Minor penetration on the front waist can be fixed by slight dragging.

This completes the hanging pants; finally, improve quality.

Next, I will teach you how to make a folded shirt stacked effect.

First, import the finished shirt.

As before, adjust the particle distance and collision thickness.

Additionally, enable the “grid display” (nine-grid) to assist with folding by providing line guides to find symmetrical positions.

I have pre-adjusted the shirt’s particle distance and collision thickness.

Also, adjust the buttons.

Our inner and outer plackets are not connected by buttons; buttons are fixed only on the outer placket, and the plackets are sewn together for stability.

Button collision is turned off.

Remove the avatar, then use the 3D garment folding tool to lay the shirt flat by rotating along the X-axis.

It may look distorted at first.

Set folding physical properties and simulate to flatten the entire garment.

After flattening, adjust the position in the 2D window, especially opening the sleeves to facilitate folding.

If some parts are bent or off-center, adjust to center them for easier folding.

Adjust the flat effect, including the collar and shoulders to reduce bulk in the middle.

If sleeves have wrinkles, gently pull and adjust.

After adjusting, use horizontal flip to turn the shirt inside out for folding, similar to real-life folding.

After final positioning, use the folding tool (default selected tool).

Click to start, hold to create a vertical fold line.

A fold ring appears; drag the arrow to fold.

Next, fold the sleeves.

Use the folding selection tool to select the sleeve panel.

Press Enter, then draw the fold line.

Only the selected panel folds.

Fold the sleeve over.

Simulate and adjust the fold position.

Add pins to prevent unfolding.

Pull the sides up and down to make the sleeve fit better.

After adjustment, remove pins.

Repeat the same on the other sleeve.

Use the folding selection tool, select the other sleeve panel, draw fold line, fold, simulate, and adjust.

When adjusting, lift the fabric to avoid contact with layers below, then move it into place for easier adjustment.

If needed, add pins for assistance.

After folding sleeves, proceed to the next fold.

Use the folding tool to fold the cuff inward at about one-third of the sleeve length.

Draw the fold line and fold.

Simulate briefly to avoid fabric slipping.

At about half the total length, draw a new fold line and fold.

Simulate again.

This completes the initial folded shirt.

Flip the shirt back using horizontal flip.

Simulate to make the form more natural.

Cancel folding physical properties to apply the fabric’s original physical properties and simulate again.

Add pins to adjust the overall fold effect, gently pulling to prevent slipping.

Add pins inside folds to tighten.

Do the same on the other side.

After adjustment, improve garment quality and simulate again.

After simulation, remove pins to allow natural movement.

If needed, make minor manual adjustments to the fold shape.

If the collar is uneven, pull gently to smooth it.

Also adjust button placket if crooked.

Because the shirt is stacked, adjust gently to avoid breaking the folded shape.

After finishing, turn off the grid.

Next, I will teach you how to make shirts folded and stacked together.

First, copy the shirt.

Freeze the bottom layer of the shirt to speed up simulation and reduce lag.

Start simulation—the many layers and overlapping can cause slow simulation.

Freeze the simulated version, then start simulation again without freezing.

When the shirt falls to the bottom layer, remove it.

Simulate the entire stack to get a natural layered effect.

Add another shirt layer on top by copying.

In the 3D window, use the positioning tool to select all shirt layers and move them close together.

Take the front one and adjust similarly.

Repeat for other layers, increasing modeling speed.

Slow down the simulation for layered sleeves.

Simulate so layers naturally fall.

Activate all layers and simulate.

Press the middle layer to create overlapping.

Freeze the bottom and simulate again.

Repeat for multiple layers to create natural stacking.

Adjust positioning so layers overlap slightly for realism.

Select two layers, move and stack together.

Position the middle layer slightly higher.

Finally, place the top shirt layer stacked on top.

The shirt stack is complete.

Apply fabric coloring as desired.

If buttons penetrate, use panel lines to fix.

That completes the stacked shirts.

You can try this later.

Next, I will teach you how to create a dressing effect where half the top is tucked into pants.

Import the finished top and pants.

Adjust particle distance and collision thickness.

Set surface offset to zero.

Group the pants, top panels, sleeves, and collar for easy selection.

This grouping helps when adjusting looseness and layers.

Activate pants and hide them.

Simulate.

Adjust looseness of the top to tighten it for a close-fit effect.

Hide pants.

Set a small rule area where the top is tucked in.

Do not set a large area to avoid insufficient motion causing clothes to run outside pants.

Keep the rule small and centered.

Continue reducing looseness for a tighter fit.

Adjust tail shrinkage to tuck the clothes outside the pants.

Use selection tool to adjust position during shrinking to prevent pulling down.

Adjust length and position.

Freeze pants and simulate to prevent clothes running outside.

Add pants layers and simulate for integrated natural effect.

After simulation, freeze pants again.

Set shrinkage back and relax looseness.

Adjust position to prevent clothes falling into pants.

Shrink in 10% increments, simulating each time.

Avoid large adjustments to prevent garment explosion.

Continue until 100%, simulating each time.

Adjust tilt slowly to avoid holes.

If holes appear, adjust accordingly.

Finally, simulate at 100%.

This completes the effect.

Show pants, simulate again.

Adjust model posture if needed by downloading poses from official website.

Apply poses and simulate again for better effect.

Hide pants if needed.

If clothes are hard to drag out, add pins in the middle.

Hide pants and adjust from inside view.

Adjust fabric to improve fit.

After finishing, delete pins and simulate naturally.

Check for penetration and adjust by dragging fabric.

Hide avatar if needed.

Adjust pins if blocking fabric.

Use reverse activation if necessary.

After final simulation, improve quality.

This completes the dressing effect.

Thank you for watching this live broadcast.

chunks.content: ## Garment Presentation Techniques in CLO Master Express This document covers detailed procedures and technical tips for creatively displaying virtual garments in CLO Master Express, focusing on hanging garments, clipped pants, folded shirts, stacked shirts, and dressing effects. Key terms include particle distance, collision thickness, folding physical properties, pins, avatar collision offset, and fabric simulation. --- ## Hanging Garments on a Hanger This section explains how to position and simulate upper garments on hangers using particle distance and collision adjustments, simulation techniques, and fabric manipulation to avoid garment-hanger penetration. ### Procedure 1. **Import Garment:** Load the finished upper garment into CLO. 2. **Adjust Simulation Parameters:** - Set particle distance to 10. - Increase collision thickness to 2. These settings speed up simulation and facilitate garment hanging. 3. **Simulate Garment:** Run simulation with adjusted parameters. 4. **Import Hanger:** Choose a hanger from CLO's system-provided options. 5. **Position Garment:** Use positioning tools to place the garment onto the hanger. 6. **Simulate on Hanger:** Start simulation, observe garment behavior. 7. **Fix Penetrations:** - If garment penetrates hanger, use the move tool to gently drag fabric outward. - Adjust shoulder areas or hanging position as needed for realistic drape. ### Notes - Proper simulation parameter adjustment is critical to balance speed and accuracy. - Slight positional tweaks during simulation improve visual quality. --- ## Creating Pants Clipped onto a Hanger This section details how to simulate jeans clipped onto a hanger using folding tools, pins, collision adjustments, and avatar offset to achieve realistic hanging effects. ### Initial Setup 1. **Import Pants:** Load finished jeans. 2. **Adjust Parameters:** Set particle distance to 10 and collision thickness to 2 for main body. 3. **Simulate and Remove Avatar:** Run initial simulation, then delete the avatar for further adjustments. 4. **Lay Pants Flat:** - Use the 3D garment folding tool. - Rotate pants along the X-axis to center on the floor. - Enable folding physical properties for softness. - Simulate until pants lay flat, including the waistband with front and back overlap. 5. **Disable Folding Properties:** After flattening, turn off folding physical properties to restore original fabric behavior. ### Hanging on Clips 1. **Import Clip Hanger:** Select hanger with clips. 2. **Position Pants:** From front view, align pants’ panels with hanger clips. 3. **Zoom and Fine-tune:** Adjust waistband and front waist positions carefully to avoid penetration. 4. **Pinning:** - Add pins in the 3D window to mark pin locations. - Use lasso pin tool to select curved waistband including label and all layers (outer, inner, pants). - Pin both sides of waistband on clips. - Add pins on side seams and above waistband to straighten pant sides. 5. **Simulation and Avatar Offset:** - Simulate; if clip area fabric moves excessively, adjust avatar surface distance (collision offset) by multiplying it by 3 and resetting to zero. - This creates more space for fabric simulation around clips. 6. **Penetration Fixes:** - Use move tool to drag fabric out of penetration.

chunks.content: - Use pins to prevent unfolding during simulation. 9. **Fold Cuffs:** - Fold cuff inward at one-third sleeve length. - Draw fold lines and simulate shortly. - Repeat fold at half sleeve length. 10. **Finalize Fold:** - Flip shirt back to normal. - Cancel folding physical properties to restore original fabric physics. - Simulate again. - Add pins inside folds to tighten and prevent slipping. - Adjust collar and button placket for evenness. - Remove grid display. ### Stacking Multiple Shirts 1. **Copy Shirt:** Duplicate folded shirt layer. 2. **Freeze Bottom Layer:** Speeds simulation and reduces lag. 3. **Simulate Stack:** Let layers fall naturally. 4. **Add Layers:** Repeat copying and positioning to build stack. 5. **Adjust Overlaps:** Slightly offset layers for realism. 6. **Simulate Slowly:** Slow simulation improves natural fall of layered sleeves. 7. **Freeze and Simulate:** Freeze lower layers between simulations to improve stability. ### Notes - Grid display assists in symmetrical folding. - Pins help maintain fold shapes during simulation. - Freezing layers enhances performance during stacking. --- ## Creating a Half-Tucked Dressing Effect This section explains how to simulate a garment tucked halfway into pants by adjusting looseness, shrinkage, layering, pins, and simulation settings. ### Setup 1. **Import Top and Pants:** Load finished top and pants. 2. **Adjust Parameters:** - Set particle distance and collision thickness appropriately. - Set surface offset to zero. 3. **Group Panels:** Group pants, top panels, sleeves, and collar for easy selection. 4. **Hide Pants and Simulate:** Simulate top alone initially. ### Tucking Procedure 1. **Adjust Looseness:** Gradually reduce looseness to achieve a close fit. 2. **Set Rule Area:** Define a small, centered rule area for tucking; avoid large areas to prevent motion errors. 3. **Shrink Tail:** Use tail shrinkage to tuck top outside pants. 4. **Manual Positioning:** Use selection tools to adjust position during shrinking to avoid pulling down. 5. **Freeze Pants:** Freeze pants layer to avoid clothes moving outside pants. 6. **Add Pants Layers:** Add pants layers and simulate for integrated effect. 7. **Adjust Shrinkage:** Incrementally increase shrinkage in 10% steps, simulating at each step. 8. **Slow Tilting:** Adjust tilt slowly to avoid fabric holes. 9. **Final Simulation:** Simulate at 100% shrinkage for final effect. ### Post-Processing 1. **Show Pants and Resimulate:** Ensure correct overlay. 2. **Apply Poses:** Download and apply poses for better posture and simulate again. 3. **Add Pins if Needed:** Pins in the middle help if fabric is difficult to drag. 4. **Hide Pants for Adjustment:** Adjust fabric from inside view for better fit. 5. **Remove Pins:** After final adjustment, delete pins and simulate naturally. 6. **Penetration Fixes:** Drag fabric, hide avatar if needed, and use reverse avatar activation if necessary. 7. **Improve Quality:** Final quality simulation completes the effect. ### Notes - Small incremental adjustments avoid garment explosions. - Grouping facilitates targeted adjustments. - Pins assist difficult fabric manipulation during fitting. --- ## Summary This lesson presents comprehensive methods for presenting virtual garments in CLO Master Express, including hanging, clipping, folding, stacking, and dressing effects.
